verdict.root_cause: productcatalogservice is deliberately failing a fraction of GetProduct requests because its 'fail' feature flag is enabled. Frontend gRPC client logs show status 13 INTERNAL with a details string generated by the catalog service naming that enabled fail flag [tr_a4ba1bf91bf1], and traces place the ERROR marking on the productcatalogservice GetProduct server span itself, with its only child (FeatureFlagService/GetFlag) returning cleanly [tr_d94a7b0bbf19]. Failures are fast rejections (~2.4ms), not timeouts, and catalog error ratio rose from a flat-zero baseline to ~9% peak with a change point at 16:54:15Z [tr_ff31c52b5213]. The wrong value is a flag whose enabled state is what breaks each affected request.
verdict.reasoning: Frontend errors are raised on the grpc-js status-receive path, so frontend surfaced a status the peer returned rather than originating it [tr_a4ba1bf91bf1], and frontend has no recorded change of any kind in the 24h covering onset [tr_37174b576e12] — so frontend is the noticer, not the cause. Traces independently confirm the error status is set on the productcatalogservice span with a healthy downstream child, excluding dependency propagation; span durations match healthy traces, excluding dependency_latency and saturation [tr_d94a7b0bbf19]. No deploy or image rollout for productcatalogservice exists in the window, excluding bad_deploy, and the only recorded changes are a traffic-shaping sidecar attached and removed ~10.8h before onset [tr_3f43548041cd]. A partial ~1% mean failure rate also explains why user-visible catalog errors fired while frontend's aggregate error ratio did not rise. What remains is a configuration value that is itself wrong; turning the flag off is the fix.
open_questions: No change record shows the fail flag being enabled — who flipped it, when, and in which system is unestablished [tr_3f43548041cd].
productcatalogservice's own logs were never read: the Loki selector used a hyphenated label and returned zero lines [tr_32613b039d16].
Trace coverage skipped 16:54–16:55 and frontend logs were truncated [tr_d94a7b0bbf19, tr_a4ba1bf91bf1], so the exact onset minutes are inferential.

alternatives.root_cause: featureflagservice holds the wrong flag value and is serving it to productcatalogservice; the edit belongs there.
alternatives.why_not: GetFlag returned successfully in ~2.1ms with no error [tr_d94a7b0bbf19]; the flag store behaved as designed. This is more likely the location of the remediating edit than a distinct fault, and no dispatch examined it.

alternatives.root_cause: An organic defect in productcatalogservice's GetProduct path returns INTERNAL intermittently, with a misleading error string.
alternatives.why_not: The GetFlag child span appears only under the errored GetProduct call and not under the nine healthy ones [tr_d94a7b0bbf19], indicating a flag-conditioned path rather than random failure; and no deploy exists to roll back to [tr_3f43548041cd].

proposal.expected_effect: No action is proposed, so no change in any metric should be observed. The catalog error ratio should continue to show intermittent STATUS_CODE_ERROR on hipstershop.ProductCatalogService/GetProduct at up to ~9%, and frontend logs should continue to emit 'Error: 13 INTERNAL: ProductCatalogService Fail Feature Flag Enabled'. The gating observation a human should collect next is a Loki query using the correct label value ({service="productcatalogservice"}, not the hyphenated variant that returned zero lines) plus a change-history read on the feature-flag store, to establish where and when the fail flag was set.
proposal.if_wrong: This abstention is wrong if a change record for the fail flag is produced — i.e. change history for productcatalogservice (or for the feature-flag store) shows a prior configuration and a flag mutation inside the incident window. That would satisfy revert_config's two preconditions and make a config_revert on productcatalogservice the right proposal. It is also wrong if the error ratio climbs materially above the observed ~9% peak or the failures become total, in which case waiting for provenance costs more than acting. Note the diagnosis itself is not what I dispute: the evidence for the mechanism is strong ([tr_a4ba1bf91bf1], [tr_d94a7b0bbf19]); what is missing is the recorded prior state that the permitted action requires.
proposal.risk: The risk of abstaining is that the deliberate failure continues: roughly 1% mean and 9% peak of GetProduct calls keep returning INTERNAL to frontend, and product-detail page errors persist for however long the flag stays enabled. Against that, the risk of proposing revert_config anyway is concrete: [tr_3f43548041cd] records only two traffic-shaping container events for productcatalogservice and explicitly no config or flag mutation in the window, so 'restore the previous configuration' has no recorded prior state to restore to — it would recreate the container against whatever the change log holds, possibly reapplying the 300ms egress-delay-era environment or a stale dependency address, turning a 9% partial failure into a broader latency or connectivity fault. Restart is also wrong here: the evidence points at a flag value, not process state, and [tr_a4ba1bf91bf1] rules out crash-loop and resource exhaustion; a restart would discard cache and very likely leave the flag enabled, producing a confusing partial recovery. Rollback fails its precondition too — no deploy or image change appears in the window.
proposal.blast_radius: If the abstention holds, the people who keep seeing it are the current sufferers: frontend (and through it loadgenerator's user journeys) on the GetProduct path, and the two services reached from productcatalogservice, checkoutservice and recommendationservice, which see the same intermittent INTERNAL on catalog reads. Had a revert_config been executed instead, the blast radius would have been productcatalogservice's container recreate — a connection reset seen by frontend, checkoutservice and recommendationservice as inbound callers — plus, if the reverted values include a dependency address, traffic movement onto whatever peer that address names, including featureflagservice, which is outside the incident's legal target set and therefore outside what this system may safely perturb.

triage_judgement.reasoning: Critical alerts across loadgenerator, frontend, and productcatalogservice within 30 seconds suggest a real user-facing failure, not a single quiet warning. Ordering points at productcatalogservice as the shared dependency behind frontend degradation, so start there.
